      <navPoint id="num_165" playOrder="165" class="chapter">

        <content src="text/part0145.html"/>
      </navPoint>
      <navPoint id="num_166" playOrder="166" class="chapter">
        <navLabel>
          <text>Opening Yourself Up to Growth</text>
        </navLabel>
        <content src="text/part0146.html"/>
        <navPoint id="num_167" playOrder="167" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>The First Dilemma. Imagine you’ve applied to graduate school. You applied to just one place because it was the school you had your heart set on. And you were confident you’d be accepted since many people considered your work in your field to be original and exciting. But you were rejected.</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0146.html#sigil_toc_id_164"/>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_168" playOrder="168" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>The Fixed-Mindset Reaction. At first you tell yourself that it was extremely competitive, so it doesn’t really reflect on you. They probably had more first-rate applicants than they could accept. Then the voice in your head starts in. It tells you that you’re fooling yourself, rationalizing. It tells you that the admissions committee found your work mediocre. After a while, you tell yourself it’s probably true. The work is probably ordinary, pedestrian, and they’d seen that. They were experts. T</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0146.html#sigil_toc_id_165"/>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_169" playOrder="169" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>The Growth-Mindset Step. Think about your goal and think about what you could do to stay on track toward achieving it. What steps could you take to help yourself succeed? What information could you gather?</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0146.html#sigil_toc_id_166"/>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_170" playOrder="170" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>Plans That You’ll Carry Out and Ones That You Won’t</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0147.html"/>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_171" playOrder="171" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>Feeling Bad, But Doing Good</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0148.html"/>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_172" playOrder="172" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>The Number One Draft Choice</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0149.html"/>
          <navPoint id="num_173" playOrder="173" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Second Dilemma. The pressure is overwhelming. You yearn for playing time in the games, but every time they put you in a game to try you out, you turn anxious and lose your focus. You were always cool under pressure, but this is the pros. Now all you see are giant guys coming toward you—twelve hundred pounds of giant guys who want to take you apart. Giant guys who move faster than you ever thought possible. You feel cornered…helpless.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0149.html#sigil_toc_id_170"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_174" playOrder="174" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Fixed-Mindset Reaction. You torture yourself with the idea that a quarterback is a leader and you’re no leader. How could you ever inspire the confidence of your teammates when you can’t get your act together to throw a good pass or scramble for a few yards? To make things worse, the sportscasters keep asking, What happened to the boy wonder?</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0149.html#sigil_toc_id_171"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_175" playOrder="175" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Growth-Mindset Step. In the growth mindset, you tell yourself that the switch to the professionals is a huge step, one that takes a lot of adjustment and a lot of learning. There are many things you couldn’t possibly know yet and that you’d better start finding out about.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0149.html#sigil_toc_id_172"/>
          </navPoint>
        </navPoint>
      </navPoint>
      <navPoint id="num_176" playOrder="176" class="chapter">
        <navLabel>
          <text>People Who Don’t Want to Change</text>
        </navLabel>
        <content src="text/part0150.html"/>
        <navPoint id="num_177" playOrder="177" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>Entitlement: The World Owes You</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0150.html#sigil_toc_id_174"/>
          <navPoint id="num_178" playOrder="178" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Next Dilemma. “Here I am,” you think, “in this low-level job. It’s demeaning. With my talent I shouldn’t have to work like this. I should be up there with the big boys, enjoying the good life.” Your boss thinks you have a bad attitude. When she needs someone to take on more responsibilities, she doesn’t turn to you. When it’s time to give out promotions, she doesn’t include you.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0150.html#sigil_toc_id_175"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_179" playOrder="179" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Fixed-Mindset Reaction. “She’s threatened by me,” you say bitterly. Your fixed mindset is telling you that, because of who you are, you should automatically be thrust into the upper levels of the business. In your mind, people should see your talents and reward you. When they don’t, it’s not fair. Why should you change? You just want your due.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0150.html#sigil_toc_id_176"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_180" playOrder="180" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Growth-Mindset Step. But first, let’s be clear. For a long time, it’s frightening to think of giving up the idea of being superior. An ordinary, run-of-the-mill human being isn’t what you want to be. How could you feel good about yourself if you’re no more valuable than the people you look down on?</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0150.html#sigil_toc_id_177"/>
          </navPoint>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_181" playOrder="181" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>Denial: My Life Is Perfect</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0151.html"/>
          <navPoint id="num_182" playOrder="182" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Dilemma. You seem to have everything. You have a fulfilling career, a loving marriage, wonderful children, and devoted friends. But one of those things isn’t true. Unbeknownst to you, your marriage is ending. It’s not that there haven’t been signs, but you chose to misinterpret them. You were fulfilling your idea of the “man’s role” or the “woman’s role,” and couldn’t hear your partner’s desire for more communication and more sharing of your lives. By the time you wake up and take notice, it</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0151.html#sigil_toc_id_179"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_183" playOrder="183" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Fixed-Mindset Reaction. You’ve always felt sorry for divorced people, abandoned people. And now you’re one of them. You lose all sense of worth. Your partner, who knew you intimately, doesn’t want you anymore.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0151.html#sigil_toc_id_180"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_184" playOrder="184" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Growth-Mindset Step. First, it’s not that the marriage, which you used to think of as inherently good, suddenly turned out to have been all bad or always bad. It was an evolving thing that had stopped developing for lack of nourishment. You need to think about how both you and your spouse contributed to this, and especially about why you weren’t able to hear the request for greater closeness and sharing.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0151.html#sigil_toc_id_181"/>
          </navPoint>
        </navPoint>
      </navPoint>
      <navPoint id="num_185" playOrder="185" class="chapter">
        <navLabel>
          <text>Changing Your Child’s Mindset</text>
        </navLabel>
        <content src="text/part0152.html"/>
        <navPoint id="num_186" playOrder="186" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>The Precocious Fixed Mindsetter</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0153.html"/>
          <navPoint id="num_187" playOrder="187" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Dilemma. Imagine your young son comes home from school one day and says to you, “Some kids are smart and some kids are dumb. They have a worse brain.” You’re appalled. “Who told you that?” you ask him, gearing up to complain to the school. “I figured it out myself,” he says proudly. He saw that some children could read and write their letters and add a lot of numbers, and others couldn’t. He drew his conclusion. And he held fast to it.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0153.html#sigil_toc_id_184"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_188" playOrder="188" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Growth-Mindset Step. You decide that, rather than trying to talk him out of the fixed mindset, you have to live the growth mindset. At the dinner table each evening, you and your partner structure the discussion around the growth mindset, asking each child (and each other): “What did you learn today?” “What mistake did you make that taught you something?” “What did you try hard at today?” You go around the table with each question, excitedly discussing your own and one another’s effort, stra</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0153.html#sigil_toc_id_185"/>
          </navPoint>
        </navPoint>
        <navPoint id="num_189" playOrder="189" class="chapter">
          <navLabel>
            <text>Effort Gone Awry</text>
          </navLabel>
          <content src="text/part0154.html"/>
          <navPoint id="num_190" playOrder="190" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Dilemma. You’re proud of your daughter. She’s at the top of her class and bringing home straight A’s. She’s a flute player studying with the best teacher in the country. And you’re confident she’ll get into the top private high school in the city. But every morning before school, she gets an upset stomach, and some days she throws up. You keep feeding her a blander and blander diet to soothe her sensitive stomach, but it doesn’t help. It never occurs to you that she’s a nervous wreck.</text>
            </navLabel>
            <content src="text/part0154.html#sigil_toc_id_187"/>
          </navPoint>
          <navPoint id="num_191" playOrder="191" class="chapter">
            <navLabel>
              <text>The Fixed-Mindset Reactions. The counselor tells you to ease up on your daughter: Let her know it’s okay not to work so hard. Make sure she gets more sleep. So you, dutifully following the instructions, make sure she gets to sleep by ten o’clock each night. But this only makes things worse. She now has less time to accomplish all the things that are expected of her.</text>
            </navLabel>
